subsubtopic: SUGGESTION GOVERNMENT HIRE CASUALS THROUGH MANPOWER RATHER THAN PRIVATE AGENCIES-MOTION UNDER S.O. 43
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I rise under the provisions of Standing Order 43 to ask the unanimous consent of the House to deal with a matter of urgent and pressing necessity. In view of the fact that as an austerity measure the government has dropped a program which would have saved millions of dollars by eliminating the government's dependence on private employment agencies to provide casual labour in the government; in view of the fact that as many as 2,000 people a day are hired through these agencies to provide casual labour for the government; and in view of the fact that these people are viciously exploited by these private companies to the extent of 20 or 30 per cent of their salaries being paid to
these companies who do no more work than accepting and making a phone call, this labour arrangement looking more like feudalism and indentured labour than anything else, I move, seconded by the hon. member for New Westminster (Mr. Leggatt):
That to protect people from exploitation at the hands of private employment firms and to save the government millions of dollars, the government immediately initiate a policy of hiring casual employees only through Canada Manpower.

EFFECT OF ENERGY COSTS IN THE ATLANTIC REGION ON FEDERAL DEVELOPMENT PROGRAMS-MOTION UNDER S.O. 43
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I rise to present a motion of urgent and pressing necessity. I think all hon. members know the devastating effect that recent large increases in costs of energy have had on the Atlantic provinces. As 90 per cent of the energy used in that part of Canada is derived from petroleum and as energy costs in the Atlantic provinces are two or three times greater than energy costs in Ontario and Quebec, I would move, seconded by the hon. member for Dartmouth-Halifax East (Mr. Forrestall):
That the Minister of Regional Economic Expansion report to this House forthwith on the negative impact on federal programs of regional development which present and increasing energy costs have; and, further, that the Minister of Energy, Mines and Resources indicate at that time what interim programs and assistance are being provided so as to ensure the effectiveness of present federal development policies and programs.

speakerposition: Minister responsible for the Status of Women; Minister of Amateur Sport; Minister of National Health and Welfare
subtopic: HEALTH AND WELFARE
subsubtopic: STATEMENT OF MINISTER ON FLU VACCINE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I would like to inform the House that my department has accepted the recommendations of the National Advisory Committee on Immunizing Agents for a selective immunization of high risk groups of Canadians against the A/Swine strain of influenza.
The Committee recommended that:
1)	Bivalent A/Swine and A/Victoria influenza vaccine be made available to those of all ages who have such chronic conditions as heart disease, chronic bronchopulmonary disease, chronic renal disease, diabetes mellitus and other chronic metabolic disorders, and to all persons over 65 years of age.
2)	Monovalent A/Swine influenza vaccine be made available for persons between the ages of 20 and 50 (highest risk 20-40 years of age) with priority being given to those responsible for maintenance of essential services.
3)	A/Swine influenza vaccine is not recommended as a routine for infants and children because of the increased incidence and severity of adverse reactions to the vaccine in those under the age of 16 years.
All provinces have accepted in principle the recommendations of the National Advisory Committee. Discussions are continuing with various manufacturers and the United States government on the availability of vaccine supplies.
In discussions with the provinces, my department offered to take responsibility for locating vaccine supplies and negotiating purchases. Because of a limited domestic capability to produce flu vaccine, it is anticipated that Canada may have to import the majority of doses.
While it is impossible to say for certain that an epidemic of A/Swine influenza will occur in the fall of 1976, the National Advisory Committee was of the opinion further A/Swine influenza virus infections in humans are possible and even likely to occur in the next year. On all previous occasions when a major new strain of influenza A virus has become established, epidemics or pandemics have resulted.
In mid-February 1976 a virus strain of A/Swine influenza was identified from four men at Fort Dix, New Jersey. This virus strain is similar to that which is suspected to have been responsible for the 1918-19 influenza pandemic which infected an estimated 500 million people worldwide, including one of every six Canadians, and resulted in

approximately 20 million deaths, including 45,000 in Canada. Since the first isolation at Fort Dix, one of the four men has died and there is now laboratory confirmation that 21 per cent of the total personnel have been infected with this virus.
Officials of my department have been in close touch with their American counterparts and are fully informed of the situation in the United States. Contact has also been made with the World Health Organization in Geneva, the WHO World Influenza Centre in London, England, and U.K. health authorities on this matter.
Vaccines to prevent influenza have been available for 40 years, and with technological advances, their efficacy has increased. A specific vaccine will provide maximum protection only against the virus strain from which it is prepared, and less protection against closely related virus strains. Protection commences approximately three weeks after vaccination.
During the past winter, influenza B, which is considered to be a less severe illness than influenza A, has been common in Canada, and is, therefore, not anticipated in epidemic proportions in the 1976-77 season. However, clinical illness due to A/Victoria/75 is currently being experienced in Canada, and it is too early to determine how many will have been infected, and conversely, how many Canadians remain susceptible. For this reason it is likely that a further outbreak of A/Victoria influenza may be experienced in Canada during the 1976-77 influenza season. It is therefore important that those high risk population groups for whom influenza vaccine has been recommended in the past, should be offered protection against the A/Victoria strain.
Similarly, the apparent absence of A/Swine influenza infection in humans in Canada since the 1918-19 pandemic has led to the development of a large population susceptible to the A/Swine virus. The New Jersey experience has demonstrated that this virus now has previously unrecognized capabilities of human-to-human transmission.
Influenza vaccine is prepared from fertilized chicken eggs infected with influenza virus. The virus in the vaccine is inactivated with formalin and thus the vaccine is known as a "killed vaccine". Immunization with a killed vaccine does not involve injection of live virus into the recipient. In the past, adverse reactions to influenza vaccine have occurred with some frequency, particularly in infants and young children. Although these reactions have been considerably reduced by new production methods, it is not advisable to recommend large scale routine immunization in this group.
In the light of the 1918 influenza pandemic experience in which individuals 20-50 years of age experienced the highest mortality rates, such persons are again considered to be at similar risk to infection from A/Swine and in need of protection.
The elderly and chronically ill require routine protection annually against the prevailing influenza strain-in this case A/Victoria. In addition, the elderly, who either escaped infection in 1918-19 outbreak, or whose immunity levels are inadequate, should receive protection against swine influenza. Hence the recommendation for the use of bivalent vaccine in this group.
March 30, 1976

A selective immunization program for high risk groups of Canadians should provide adequate protection for the public and, in addition, help to reduce the potential of worldwide spread of influenza A/Swine virus. The high degree of cooperation already evident in federal-provincial discussions on this matter indicates that the immunization program should be successful in achieving these goals.
Mr. Speaker, with the permission of the House and in view of the exceptional circumstances of this case, I would like to table in English and in French, a copy of the report of the National Advisory Committee on Immunizing Agents.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, before I get into the meat of this statement I want to express some displeasure about the fact that the minister provided a copy of his comments only very shortly before the sitting began. It is impossible to make a detailed study of the announcement in such a short space of time. Further, it is rather strange he should have chosen not to let us see the report of the National Advisory Committee on Immunizing Agents, but that he should simply have tabled it at the end of his comments. The minister points to the report now, but he sees I am on my feet and obviously I cannot look at the report or study it.
Having said that, I agree that a vigorous national immunization program should be undertaken. I am somewhat confused by a number of statements the minister has been making on this subject in the past few days as well as today. He tells us a selective program was chosen, but he does not give us the reasons for making this choice rather than opting for the innoculation of the total population as the Americans have decided to do. Had I seen the advisory committee's report in advance, I might have got the answer from that report. But since I did not have that opportunity I shall have to make my comments on the basis of the statements which the minister made.
On March 25, in response to a question from my hon. friend from Simcoe North (Mr. Rynard) the minister told the House that Canada has the capacity to produce 300,000 vaccine doses by next fall. That number coincides, incidentally, with a press report suggesting that the Armand Frappier Institute, University of Quebec, is capable of producing that number of doses. The minister also suggests that the majority of the vaccine to be used here would have to be imported from the United States. Yet in a telephone interview with Dr. Salk, the man famous for having developed the polio vaccine-he is now the director of a large U.S. government viral research establishment-expressed the opinion that the United States would not have any of this vaccine available for export until November, which would be too late for us. Another press report suggests that the United States might find it difficult to find enough vaccine to meet its own needs.
Further to this, I have information from Connaught Laboratories suggesting that if the department of national health gave them the go-ahead, so to speak, they would be capable of obtaining machinery which could produce between five million and ten million doses in this country by the end of the year. It is strange the minister chose not to
Flu Vaccine
mention anything about that. Perhaps we can conclude from his utterances in the past few days that he only went to the Armand Frappier Institute and did not bother to ask Connaught what they could do. Apparently Connaught has an option on some special machinery which could produce these large numbers of doses for us; this machinery could be purchased. They had some reservations about the availability of eggs, and we could possibly enlist the help of the Minister of Agriculture (Mr. Whelan) as far as eggs are concerned; he has recently had some problems disposing of them.
The statement made by the minister is woefully lacking with respect to certain information. Additional information must be provided in order that the House might appreciate the problem the hon. gentleman is facing. Perhaps we could then understand why the figure he has given us seems to be at such variance with the figures I have been able to obtain with respect to our production capability. The minister suggests that those between the ages of 20 and 50 would be given A swine vaccine and that those who are suffering from debilitating illnesses, and all those over 65, would be given a combined vaccine of A swine virus and A Victoria virus. This leaves a substantial segment of our population unprotected-all those between the ages of 50 and 65 and all those under the age of 16.
In the same statement the minister says the vaccine is not being given to those under the age of 16 because of the possibility of adverse reactions. Yet children under the age of 16 who are ill will be given it. This suggests to me that perhaps the danger from an adverse reaction is less than the danger of the disease itself. Maybe an explanation should be given us with regard to this point. We know from past experience, from the experience in New Jersey, that this virus is transmittable from human to human, and it is therefore important that all who live in this country should be protected to the best of our capability. We find in the minister's statement the suggestion that there is a large reservoir of susceptible people, a situation which calls for the placing of greater emphasis on a more comprehensive immunization program.
One of the questions I want to put to the minister is this: Who is to bear the cost of the administration of this program? I believe the minister told us earlier that the federal government would pay for the vaccine and that perhaps the provincial governments would bear the cost of administration and distribution. But he made no further comment on that aspect today. He told us, however, that in addition to those in the various age groups who would be protected, those responsible for the maintenance of essential services would also be vaccinated. I wonder what he means by that, precisely.
When we talk on other subjects and try to determine what essential services are, the government always pleads total ignorance. I am interested in finding out what these essential services are. I wonder whether members of the government of Canada will be included. It occurs to me we might find the country runs much better without the government of Canada than with it. In any case, we shall have an opportunity to question the minister a little later. In the meantime, perhaps he will give serious thought to the questions I have raised so he can deal with them in a few minutes' time.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, in reply to the statement that the minister just made, concerning the intentions of the government of Canada as to the A/swine influenza, I wish to point out that I am glad to hear such statements today. This shows that the Department of National Health is concerned at this moment about the problem raised by the reappearance of that virus which seamingly was responsible for the pandemic called the Spanish flu in 1918-19.
The minister points out in thinly veiled terms the possible severeness of the situation, especially if it were to make any progress, since every time there was that A/swine influenza, epidemics occurred whith the terrible effects we know. It must be considered that our bodies no longer have the necessary resources to fight effectively that disease, for it has disappeared for a long time. We know that the virus may be conveyed among human beings, but science still does not know how the disease is conveyed.
For the moment, it seems very difficult to obtain a useful stock of vaccines for Canadians. If we depend on other countries to obtain the vaccines that we lack, what will happen if those countries need them for themselves?
To emphasize the seriousness of the situation, I would like to mention two other facts. The United States have announced their intention to prepare for massive inoculation. The World Health Organization is now concentrating its energies on the problem of the reappearance of this virus. There is certainly no cause for alarm, but before such a situation, which I believe to be even more serious than the minister suggests, we must take some action. It is not unthinkable that it would become impossible to vaccinate everyone who needs it if the disease really took epidemic proportions next fall or next winter. This could certainly greatly worsen a situation which is already difficult in Canada in various aspects.
We must in fact wonder if there are not very specific causes for all this. At any rate, I urge the Minister to continue to examine this problem very seriously and with all the energy required. I believe that our governments, like the rest of Canadians, have to realize that we must unite before this problem and concentrate our efforts and allocate the money required. Later might be too late.
We hope that the Minister of National Health and Welfare (Mr. Lalonde) will study very closely the age and group selection made and recommended by the advisory group whose report has just been submitted to the House and which I have not read. In any event, we are certain that this is not a matter of politics or of saving money. We are all aware that there are much more important things at stake, and that the health of Canadians is involved.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, it would be easier for me to provide the answers to some of these questions if the hon. member did not always distort what I have said. I did not say I rejected Dr. Salk's statement; I said he was not the authority to speak on behalf of the American government. That is a very different thing. We have discussed this with United States officials. The question is being raised at a very senior level of the United States administration and I hope to have an answer on the subject in the next few days. There is no reason to believe we will not be able to count on roughly the same proportion of supply as that which we have received in the past. Frankly, there is not much point in the United States immunizing the majority of its population if there are millions of people up north of it who are not immunized at all and who might be subject to this particular influenza. It is to the advantage of all of North America to immunize as many people as possible. The selective approach within Canada has been set out by the national advisory committee on the subject.

subtopic: MEASURE TO PROHIBIT ACQUISITION OF LAND BY NON-CANADIAN CITIZENS OR LANDED IMMIGRANTS
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, the bill addresses itself to the problem of non-residents of Canada holding land here for investment purposes. The bill is called the Foreign Land Ownership Act and prohibits the acquisition of land by persons who are not Canadian citizens or landed immigrants, except for residential and recreational uses, up to a maximum of ten acres, or for the purposes of a business permitted under the terms of the Foreign Investment Review Act. This is a great problem in urban areas of Canada where non-residents tie up land, thereby increasing housing prices. The bill is addressed to that problem.

subtopic: CRIMINAL LAW AMENDMENT ACT (NO. 1), 1976 MEASURES FOR BETTER PROTECTION OF CANADIAN SOCIETY AGAINST CRIME

speechtext:
The House resumed, from Monday, March 29, consideration of the motion of Mr. Basford that Bill C-83, for the better protection of Canadian society against perpetrators of violent and other crime, be read the second time and

referred to the Standing Committee on Justice and Legal Affairs.

subtopic: CRIMINAL LAW AMENDMENT ACT (NO. 1), 1976 MEASURES FOR BETTER PROTECTION OF CANADIAN SOCIETY AGAINST CRIME
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, when we reached ten o'clock last night I was speaking on the amendment to this bill and had pointed out that in order to administer certain parts, a great number of bureaucrats would be required both for the purpose of administration and for registration of gun owners.
At this time I should like to point out that an applicant for a gun licence must obtain the signatures of two people of good character and reputation who will vouch for his or her character and undertake to provide sort of a guarantee that the gun or guns will not be used for criminal purposes. I suggest there will not be many people who will want to go that far out on the limb even for a very good friend. We have already set out the rationale for the secret possession or illegal registration of guns by those who cannot obtain such guarantees from two citizens in their community. I am sure the minister has already thought of the difficulty this could pose for a large percentage of law-abiding Canadians who will be dependent on friends or relatives regarding a gun application. The effect will be severely to limit the application of the law.
North Americans will simply not abide by a law they consider to be oppressive or against the rights of the majority. Let us take a hypothetical case of a gun owner who has his house burgled and his gun stolen and used in a subsequent crime. This happens frequently, or at least it happens often enough for us to know that criminals do not abide by gun registration laws any more than they abide by laws concerning break and entry, theft, assault, or any other law. Criminals steal weapons from police cars, police stations, armouries, and even from policemen. Requiring law-abiding citizens to register guns will not have any effect on this type of crime or this type of acquisition of guns.
Responsible gun owners do not leave their guns around for people to pick up or steal; they keep their guns secured. I do not believe anyone would object to laws concerning the safe and secure storage of guns when they are not in use. However, criminals are not respecters of that kind of security. They pick locks, knock down doors and windows; they use axes, crowbars, screwdrivers, hammers and many other tools available in every hardware store. If a housebreaker came upon a gun cabinet or closet, or guns secured by chains, he would simply use the tools of his trade to obtain the guns, just as is done to obtain money, jewels and other kinds of loot.
Chains and locks can be sawed through with a hacksaw, closets can be chopped open with hatchets and axes, doors can be forced in a variety of ways by the expert criminal. My experience as an insurance underwriter convinces me that experienced and determined housebreakers or safe crackers simply will not be stopped. The only way that I can think of to stop them is to convince them that they will be caught, convicted and imprisoned and that they will not be allowed to go out for weekends.
Mr. Speaker, in my area there are a great number of summer cottages. Many of the owners leave rifles and
March 30, 1976

shotguns there, probably because they do not want to transport them back and forth to their principal residence. Even if these are well hidden, they are the things that burglars seem to find and steal. The Ontario Provincial Police have pointed out that burglars are not interested in furniture but are usually looking for guns, whisky or any other type of alcoholic beverage.

subtopic: CRIMINAL LAW AMENDMENT ACT (NO. 1), 1976 MEASURES FOR BETTER PROTECTION OF CANADIAN SOCIETY AGAINST CRIME
speechtext: What about rum?

subtopic: CRIMINAL LAW AMENDMENT ACT (NO. 1), 1976 MEASURES FOR BETTER PROTECTION OF CANADIAN SOCIETY AGAINST CRIME
speechtext:
Rum, too. A few weeks ago there was a news item on a television news program about an upsurge in gun sales in one of the western provinces since this gun control legislation was tabled. This is a natural reaction by people who feel that their rights are being transgressed, and I would not be surprised to find that the same thing is happening right across the country. If this legislation is passed, I would also suggest that a large number of guns will not be registered.
In the Ottawa Journal of March 10 there was a supplement put out by the Canadian Tire Corporation. It was advertising a special price on a Winchester repeating rifle of $38.88, and also a special price for a rifle-scope at $10.88. That can be a pretty dangerous weapon, Mr. Speaker, if it falls into the wrong hands. I believe the same advertisement was run by Simpsons-Sears.
The gun manufacturers and their sales outlets are making capital out of this proposed legislation. Everyone that I have talked with concerning registration of gun owners has been in agreement, almost without exception, that some type of registration would be acceptable and even desirable for these weapons, but why should we set up an enormous bureaucracy to administer a registration process when we already have tens of thousands of police stations and detachments across the country? The police are responsible for public safety and security, and they would be better suited for the task of administering a gun law than an appointed official with no training or background in law enforcement.
On March 8, the member for New Westminster (Mr. Leggatt) mentioned that the Minister of Justice (Mr. Bas-ford) had stated that crime in Canada is under control, and the hon. member pointed out, astutely, that nothing could be further from the truth. Crime is not under control. It is on the rise in Canada, as elsewhere, and we cannot just sit by and say smugly that it is not as bad in Canada as it is somewhere else, Mr. Speaker. I am not interested in crime somewhere else. I am interested, and I am concerned about the rise in crime, particularly violent crime, here in Canada.
The hon. member for New Westminster pointed out that there is no mention in this bill of the serious problem of hard drugs, of how the Minister of Justice proposes to control the importation, sale and use of hard drugs in Canada which is, incidentally, one of the chief causes of all types of crime today. It is a point well taken, Mr. Speaker. I have to ask, why there is not some mention of this serious aspect of crime in this bill? Why do we not find some slight clue that the government is as interested in the causes of crime as it is in coddling criminals after they are convicted. I do not suggest that we get as tough as some countries in the world where the death penalty has been imposed for
Measures Against Crime
mere possession in an effort to stamp out this insidious and pernicious practice.
More money, more personnel and more support of every type must be put at the disposal of those charged with preventing the importation of hard drugs into Canada and to those charged with tracking down drugs and drug peddlers within our country. The penalties for trafficking and importing drugs must be made severe enough to deter the most hardened and skeptical criminals. I say skeptical because this government has earned the unenviable reputation of being soft on criminals. I do not believe that the criminal in our country today really expects to be kept in prison very long if he is convicted and sentenced. We must remove the skepticism and replace it with respect for the law and our law enforcement agencies. That respect will only come with the knowledge that we in Canada are determined to stamp out crime whenever and wherever we find it.
One provision of this bill that the majority of members will object to is the one concerning wiretapping. I believe this provision should be modified. There is no doubt that wiretapping, or the interception of telephone communications, has been and will be a most important tool in the hands of law enforcement agencies, especially in their efforts to control organized crime. Those of us who live in rural areas are quite used to having our communications intercepted, as anyone familiar with a party line telephone can attest. We are not concerned one way or the other with wiretapping legislation, but in congested urban centres it is another matter.
As long as this practice is engaged in judiciously by law enforcement agencies, with the consent of the courts as prescribed by present law, then I cannot think of any reason why the law should be relaxed. I do not think it would do much in the way of hindering investigations if the persons whose conversations are intercepted are notified of this fact within a reasonable period of time after the investigation has been completed. Perhaps we can work out some plan whereby persons who have been found to be engaged in criminal activity as a result of such taps will not have to be told of the taps while the investigation is under way.
It seems to me that within a period of 90 days the police should be able to determine whether a person is using his or her telephone in the commission of criminal activities. This requirement to disclose the use of wiretaps will limit, and possibly even prevent, indiscriminate use of this practice. While I am certainly in favour of giving our police every advantage over criminals, I also want to protect citizens' rights.
Mr. Speaker, I would like to ask why the government did not see fit to include some provisions in this bill to deal with the problem of alcoholism and its related abuses, and to comment on a couple of other problems areas. Alcoholism and drug addiction have been combined as a general problem area by most, if not all, of the agencies dealing with these problem. Like my colleague from New Westminster, I am appalled that the Minister of Justice has not seen fit to tell us that the federal government is at least as concerned about these problems as the rest of us.

March 30, 1976
Measures Against Crime
I have some startling figures with regard to the rise in the number of collisions on our highways, many of them fatal or resulting in disabling injuries, where teenage drinking drivers were involved. In 1967, in Ontario, there were 1,089 collisions on the highways involving teenage drinking drivers. The figure rose gradually for the next four years until 1971 when it almost doubled to 2,277. In 1972 it rose to 3,623. In 1974, the last year for which complete figures are available, the figure was 5,385, almost five times the number of collisions involving teenage drinking drivers in 1967.
While I realize that these figures are for Ontario, this is not something which is limited to Ontario alone. It is a national problem and as such it deserves some attention from the Minister of Justice and possibly the Solicitor General (Mr. Allmand). At least we in Ontario realize that it is a serious problem, on the basis of statistics, namely, that the age of drivers involved in collisions when impaired has dropped to the 17 and 18 year old group. The provincial government is reassessing its decision to drop to 18 the legal age for drinking. However, as I have said, this is not only an Ontario problem and I should like to see some indication that the federal government is concerned about it. It has been known for many years that every conceivable kind of drug, soft and hard, is available in our schools almost on demand, not only in high schools but in schools where the average age is from 10 years to 13 years. This is certainly an area in which the federal government could do more than it is now-but there is nothing in this bill dealing with drugs or alcohol.
Violence on television is another problem area which has not been explored or examined in depth by the federal government, despite the fact that at least 90 per cent of these violent programs are available only on the two national television networks. It has been suggested, rightly or wrongly-and I am not an expert in these matters-that violence on television can often trigger a response on the part of people who are deranged and can be encouraged to act a violent scene portrayed on a television show. This does not apply in the case of television dramas. It is believed by many competent psychiatrists and socialists that when news programs dwell unnecessarily on the gory details of a particularly horrible crime, a deranged person thousands of miles from the scene of the crime might be tempted to emulate the crime to the last detail.
I believe that the whole question of the portrayal of violence on television, in all its forms, needs to be examined in depth by a competent individual or group. We should have more information and more opinions on this subject than are available to us at the present time. I would hate to have to weigh the merits of a proposal as to how we should deal with this matter on the basis of the scant information available of the effects or possible effects this type of thing could have on the minds of the young or on the minds of deranged adults.
I recently had the opportunity of meeting, with some other hon. members, the president of the Canadian Broadcasting Corporation, Mr. A. W. Johnson. I asked him for his views on this contentious subject. He admitted he had no direct solution or answer to this problem as there were arguments on both sides. Therefore, he let the matter go on

that basis. But I certainly feel that this is worth investigating further. In the February edition of Canada Gunsport there is an article headed "Gun control fails in the United Kingdom; chief inspector admits 50 years of controls useless." In the article which follows it is stated:
We wonder if we are not asking the wrong questions. The rise in the criminal use of firearms does not appear to have been influenced in any significant way by changes in the system of firearms control.
The criminal knows that for a professional robbery the chances of detection are low and the rewards high. The maximum penalty is life imprisonment and he knows that if proven guilty he is likely to receive a substantial prison sentence. The odds against him being caught may be something like 7 or 10 to 1 in his favour. When the death penalty is applied he is not prepared to accept 7 or 10 to 1 odds on a chance of being hanged.
The article goes on-not attributing this to Chief Inspector Colin Greenwood of the West Yorkshire constabulary-to say that in Holland, where television programs such as CTV's "W-5" has held gun control up as a solution, the recent events with that train in Beilen and Amsterdam have shown that gun control has been a failure. Austria has strict firearms controls, but the attack on the OPEC meeting by terrorists in which three people were killed supports the suggestion that we are asking the wrong questions. The chief inspector also made this statement;
Guns were always available to any criminal who chose to use them. Firearms controls do not appear to stop this class of criminal from obtaining a gun when he felt that he could use one.
Then there is another reference which is certainly of interest. Meeting on December 18, the Massachusetts police chiefs' association, comprising 200 police chiefs, unanimously went on record opposing a petition being circulated to ban hand-guns, and they gave as their reason that criminals would not turn in hand-guns because the supreme court had ruled that illegal hand-guns do not have to be registered as that would amount to self-incrimination; that the majority of law abiding citizens would turn in their guns and would then be at the mercy of criminals; that the law would make criminals out of law-abiding persons who did not turn in their guns; that crime had increased dramatically and the police cannot protect everyone; and that therefore a citizen should have the right to protect his family and himself.
As a personal observation, I point out that people tend to identify with the police force and the fire department. Apparently we are good citizens if we have fire extinguishers in our homes, because we know that firemen cannot be there instantly. Apparently we are bad citizens if we have guns in our homes, although the police cannot be there instantly. The fire department does not show up until after the fire has started, and the police do not start showing any interest until after a crime has been committed.
Along with a great many other members of parliament, I have received a tremendous amount of correspondence with regard to gun control, most of it highly critical of the proposed legislation, and some of it in favour of some form of control, so it cannot be stated that we are against any form of control whatsoever. I have here a letter from a former member of the RCMP who might take a rather stronger and more severe attitude than would be acceptable to people today, but he states very strongly the importance of police departments having the facilities, manpower and everything else available for dealing with hard
March 30, 1976

drugs. He also states, in no uncertain terms, that youth and alcoholism are very important items responsible for a great deal of crime, and violent crime. He says he has reservations about wiretapping. He states:
While I never approved of wiretapping, much, RCMP did some during the second war. It is O.K. for interception of top criminals, evidence, but to me appeared a weakness, a crutch. I secured my evidence the hard way.
I do not know what he meant by that. He went on to emphasize that our soft tactics must stop; we must go after habitual criminals, see they are put away and remain put away.
Firearms control cannot even be justified with the excuse that it will reduce accidental injury and death. In Ontario, accidental hunting deaths fell from 71 in 1961 to eight in 1970. This favourable statistic is probably the result of hunter safety courses run by local anglers and hunters' associations. Nationally, our accidental death rate due to automobiles was 26.4 per 100,000 persons in 1973. Although it is estimated that there are between five million and ten million firearms in Canada, the accidental death rate due to them is so low that neither the Canada Year Book of 1973 nor the Canadiana Encyclopedia even mention it in their accidental death rate tables. The rate must be less than the last entry in the table, which was one per 100,000.
All the above information and more indicates that gun control has little or no effect on the criminal. However, gun control does severely limit the legitimate ownership and use of firearms in the hands of everyone else. Presumably, these facts are well known to the Solicitor General and the Minister of Justice.
It seems, Mr. Speaker, that criminals will always acquire weapons for crime, whether they be stolen, purchased, imported to the country or assembled in back-room workshops. Many first class firearms have been manufactured by hobbyists for legal purposes.
The Minister of Justice has stated that the availability of firearms is the major cause of crime. This has proven false. As an example he took gunless Japan, which has a low murder-arrest rate, but said nothing about Ireland which has the toughest gun laws in the world. He also said nothing about Switzerland, which has an extremely low crime rate. There it is the law that every male of military age shall keep a government-owned firearm in his home. We could solve our crime problems relatively easily, not by punishing and restraining law abiding citizens but simply by taking trouble-makers out of circulation. We can impose capital punishment on the worst offenders, and mandatory minimum prison sentences for the rest without chance of parole. They should be released when their sentence is completed.

subtopic: CRIMINAL LAW AMENDMENT ACT (NO. 1), 1976 MEASURES FOR BETTER PROTECTION OF CANADIAN SOCIETY AGAINST CRIME
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I listened with great interest to the hon. member who preceded me. This bill contains a good many provisions for combating crime. I propose to restrict my remarks to one small part of the bill, and in response to representations made to me by my constitutents I will talk about the problem of gun control.
Measures Against Crime
Let me make it clear that I support the principle of this bill. I shall vote for it on second reading and hope it will be referred at the earliest possible date to committee. It is my sincere hope that at the committee stage there will be extensive hearings which will deal with the very matters raised by those who feel they will be unfairly treated by the provisions of this bill. I am referring particularly to gun clubs and gun collectors. I am confident that the committee hearings will lead to greater acceptance of the bill because we shall recognize more clearly the problems which Canada faces.
On January 26 of this year I presented a petition to this House signed by 7,486 high school students of the city of Ottawa calling on this House to enact legislation as soon as possible to restrict the availability of firearms, so as to avoid another tragic incident similar to that which took place in an Ottawa area high school on October 27, 1975, and in Brampton on May 4, 1975. The fear of the possible recurrence of such events has created tension in the classrooms and schools of this area and has resulted in deterioration of the learning atmosphere. The petition which was organized and circulated by the students themselves called on the government to "act as quickly as possible" in enacting the necessary legislation. I am relieved to see the measure now before the House, as are many of my constituents who made their feelings known during the Christmas period by responding to a questionnaire which I circulated on a household basis on the subject of gun control.
The results showed that 83 per cent of those who responded-which is about 15 per cent of all households which received the questionnaire-favoured the registration of rifles and firearms; 88 per cent favoured the registration of hand-guns. Eighty three per cent favoured tests to satisfy reasonable standards of competence and safety for everyone owning a gun. There was virtually no opposition to the need to restrict ease of availability of firearms.
I recognize that I represent an urban constituency, and know that in many parts of Canada the tradition of ownership and responsible use of firearms is different from that in some of our larger cities. I can only speak in this House for the people who elected me and express views that I believe they would want me to express. At the same time, like other hon. members I have received a number of well prepared briefs from organizations representing gun clubs and hunters arguing that any new legislation should not violate their rights, namely, the rights of those individuals who have traditionally demonstrated respect for the proper use of firearms in the enjoyment of sport.
Responsible collectors maintain that they may be penalized by the new legislation. Collectors say they will be forced to give up all their operative automatic rifles and machine-guns under the new prohibited weapons clause. Many collections include museum pieces worth a great deal of money to their owners. Collectors have maintained to me that the firing mechanisms, if kept separate from the weapons, are almost impossible for potential thieves to obtain or duplicate. Actually, criminals invariably steal either hand-guns or high-powered rifles which they prefer to machine-guns. I shall return to that in a minute.
Some automatic rifles will not be covered by the prohibited weapons clause. It has been brought to my attention

March 30, 1976
Measures Against Crime
that semi-automatic rifles can be converted to automatic guns with relative ease by people with only limited training. I am referring specifically to the M-l semi-automatic rifle which can be obtained at many locations across Canada. I have in my possession a number of catalogues advertising semi-automatic rifles available both through mail order and for personal shoppers. For example, I have before me a supplement distributed by the Ottawa Citizen earlier this year. In it, a well known local store advertises a .22 calibre target pistol. You can go and pick it put. It suggests that a B-B gun is a nice present for a teenage son.
I am looking, as well, at a Sears' catalogue containing a section on rifles, including automatic rifles, which can be readily purchased. The advertisement says that guns and ammunition will not be sold to persons under 17. I suppose that is intented to salve someone's conscience. Yet it is clear that the public, certainly that part of it which I have the honour to represent here, wants us to restrict the ease with which firearms can be acquired.
I have another announcement in my hand which surprises me. The Globe and Mail of March 4, 1976, reports that the Sudbury police were offering pistols for sale. According to the article, the Sudbury regional police were selling about 100, .32 calibre revolves for about $25 each. The police chief said that the revolvers were originally issued to constables formerly employed by area municipalities. With the amalgamation of the forces into a regional force, the .38 special became standard, so that the .32 calibre became the property of the regional police. They were surplus, and a dollar being a dollar, why not sell them?
It is clear that we have a situation which calls for some kind of legislative restriction. I am not prepared to say that the bill in its present form cannot be improved. It will be the responsibility of hon. members who serve on the committee which looks at this bill to go over it clause by clause, to hear representations from organized groups of citizens and to ensure that the bill represents the best possible protection of the interests of the public.
I am surprised at some of the mail I receive. I have a constituent who is a postman, a letter carrier. He is a man of excellent character. I would have no hesitation in writing a character reference for him at any time. His name is Mr. Wayne Green. Mr. Green has a specialty. He has been collecting machine-guns over the past many years. He has a collection that has cost him approximately $25,000. He described to me in great detail the care that he takes, how he has registered every one of these guns with the Royal Canadian Mounted Police, and how he keeps them in an inoperable form in his home: the firing mechanisms are stored separately.
I am surprised really at this hobby, although I respect the right to a hobby. There has certainly been nothing illegal about this gentleman pursuing this kind of hobby to date. I said earlier that generally, when thieves steal guns, they do not go for this kind of weapon. I think there is a limit in terms of what the public is prepared to endure. If an underground organization wanted to acquire machine-guns, I suspect that with the use of trained people who could be placed at their disposal they could adapt these guns by reproducing the firing mechanisms. If advertised,

this kind of collection could be a target for some kind of illegal activity.
The problem of dealing with collectors will be very complicated. It may well be that there should be some phasing-out period, that the trading of guns between collectors will have to be restricted and should take place only between those who are registered and recognized as professional collectors. There may be some means by which the investment and savings of those who have chosen this kind of hobby can be given some protection. However, I have to say that I support the principle of the bill and that the public demands this kind of restriction on the availability of firearms. We have a responsibility, in light of the changing conditions of our cities and the pattern of violence that is emerging, to create for at least these parts of our country an environment in which firearms are not so readily available.
I recognize that this is a big country. I know that in the frontier, the northern areas and rural areas, the use of firearms is a very different thing. However, it is clear that for our large urban areas a measure like this will have to be enacted.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I thank hon. members for allowing me to continue the speech which I began on March 11 last and which I had not finished.
Mr. Speaker, as I was saying, if the minister wants I can give him lots of evidence. I shall read a letter I received from the Hunting and Fishing Association of Malartic:
We are against the project to control guns. We think that such a measure amounts to a lack of civic consideration towards all our sportsmen.
Francois Ferron, chairman of the Hunting and Fishing Association of Malartic.
Another group representing hundreds of sportsmen from northwest Quebec is violently opposed to the project of the Minister of Justice.
If the minister wants more, I have other examples to give him. I received a letter from Mr. Jean-Claude Bouchard, of Val-d'Or, the chairman of the Hunting and Fishing Association of this municipality.
In that letter, he asks me to help him fight Bill C-83. I was pleased to answer him that he could count on me.
I could give more examples of representations made by people from Senneterre, Chibougamau, Chapais and Cadillac, all towns where most people hunt big and small game.
March 30, 1976

And I could list several other municipalities of my constituency.
Mr. Speaker, when I comment on this bill today, I speak on behalf of the great majority of the people I represent. I know that they entirely support my efforts to bring the Minister of Justice to understand what common sense says about this Bill C-83. I speak on behalf of all those who love hunting and outdoor sports when I ask the minister to withdraw his bill and remove from it the clauses concern-irfg the control of firearms.
As do all other Canadians, people in northwest Quebec want to be protected against criminal activity. They want more severe punishment to be given to habitual criminals. I am sure they approve of the clauses of Bill C-83 which deal with the protection of society against hard-core criminals. But they do not want gun control. They know that honest citizens will be the only ones to suffer from such a measure. They ask that the residents of urban areas, where there is no hunting, make an effort to understand and respect their wishes to practice their favourite sports without being subjected to a thousand and one controls by officials.
Therefore, Mr. Speaker, I appeal to this House on behalf of all sportsmen and hunters. I ask hon. members of all parties to forget their party differences and vote against this bill which, in my estimation, will not contribute in any way to the protection of honest citizens.
Our fellow citizens are following with great interest the debate on this bill and I can assure hon. members who vote for gun controls that they will have to give accounts of their conduct in this regard. I shall be pleased to let their electors know they voted for this bill and constituents will take note of their vote.
Their constituents will not forgive them for that vote, which will penalize the sportsmen and the hunters of their regions. Mr. Speaker, government members are embarrassed at having to support such a bill. They know their voters, particularly those who represent rural constituencies, will not forgive them for supporting a bill which will oblige people to register their firearms, to wait for hours in civil servants' offices, while inspectors will check their past record to determine whether they can get a licence for their rifle or shotgun.
It is not without reason, Mr. Speaker, that many government members have tried to interrupt my speech on March 11, by making noise and putting non identifiable questions. They know I am speaking the truth and I am talking on behalf of the majority of Canadians.
Controlling firearms is not a good means of reducing crime. Let us take for instance Switzerland. In that country, all adult citizens must keep a firearm, it is provided by law. Yet that country's crime rate as regards qualified thefts and homicides is very low. Still, far from controlling firearms, Switzerland requires its citizens to possess guns and rifles.
In England, on the contrary, where gun control laws have been very tough for more than 50 years, a study conducted by Inspector Colin Greenwood of the British police force indicated that gun control did not help reduc-
Measures Against Crime
ing the number of crimes involving firearms. As a matter of fact, statistics show that the violent crime rate has increased by 400 per cent since 1963 in England, gun controls notwithstanding.
Once again, Mr. Speaker, it is obvious that such controls will not help reduce the number of violent crimes. This has been proven. The countries where there are no gun controls have very low crime rates, whereas the countries enforcing strict controls suffer increasing crime rates.
Mr. Speaker, I would like to bring forward one last argument at this point in the discussion, that is the excessive cost of this control for Canadian taxpayers. An army of public servants will be needed to register all firearms. Tons of paper will be needed to keep up to date the necessary files. Hundreds of public servants will also be needed to check whether people do have their permit and whether this permit is in fact valid. The government is now suggesting that we have to tighten our belt, and that it will reduce its own expenses. It has even announced the discontinuance of several programs aimed at helping students, old people and the unemployed to take part in useful projects.
Now he is asking us to let him spend millions to set up a program as ridiculous and as useless as gun control. If the government wishes to be consistent, it must revise its position and be aware of the fact that there is an obvious discrepancy between the stated view that government expenses will be curbed and this expensive gun control bill.
In closing, I would like to remind the House that a cabinet minister recently told Canadians that they should give up their usual life style. That minister may be right. One of the habits people ought to get rid of, and I hope for ever, is that of electing a Liberal government in Ottawa.
If the government puts forward more legislation like the gun control bill, it can be sure that Canadians will be cured of the habit they had to vote liberal.

But I think I ought to bring to the attention of this House the kind of letter which was written to my constituent, Mr. Vair, who, incidentally, represents 23,000 sportsmen. The letter is dated March 3, 1976. It starts out with the words "Mr. Vair", not "Dear Sir" or "Dear Mr. Vair". The letter goes on to say:
Your letter and bumper sticker have reached my office. The impression you intend to leave with the public that guns will be outlawed is

March 30, 1976
Measures Against Crime
the kind of narrow, distorted extremism which spreads nothing but confusion and hatred. Have you nothing better to offer as a positive contribution, or do you know what the word means?

subtopic: CRIMINAL LAW AMENDMENT ACT (NO. 1), 1976 MEASURES FOR BETTER PROTECTION OF CANADIAN SOCIETY AGAINST CRIME
speechtext:
I do not intend to reveal the name of the member who had the nerve to write such a letter. I would have hoped, however, that he would have learned by now that, regardless of political affiliation, it is incumbent to act in a manner becoming a member of parliament.
Bill C-83 embodies proposals to screen out potential misuse of guns and restrict the general availability of firearms. Some of the changes in, and additions to, the provisions of the offensive weapons section of the Criminal Code are as follows: The addition of a licensing system to apply to all persons who possess or propose to acquire firearms or ammunition, other than persons under the age of 18 and those who would be subject to special temporary permit provisions. A general strengthening of the offence provisions relating to the importation, possession, carriage, handling, storage, transfer and use of firearms and other offensive weapons and of related search and seizure provisions. Strengthening and extension of the permit provisions applicable to businesses which deal in firearms or ammunition and strengthening of the registration certificate provisions in relation to restricted weapons.
If this bill is passed, applicants for restricted weapons will in future be required to justify the need for such weapons before a certificate is granted. Police will be able to seize a weapon without a warrant in cases where there is reason to fear danger to human safety. Every possessor of a firearm will require a licence, good for five years. Such a licence will be issued only after the licensing officer finds there is nothing in the applicant's background to make him unfit to bear a weapon. Persons under 18 will require special permits issued only for target practice, game hunting and firearms instructions. One of the guarantors must be a parent or legal guardian. All firearms and ammunition dealers, traders and importers and manufacturers will be required to obtain permits and keep records of all their transactions.
Mr. Speaker, I shall now review our present gun laws with the object of showing they already meet our needs adequately. The Criminal Code lays down the law concerning the use of firearms. Weapons are defined under three categories-prohibited, restricted and unrestricted. Prohibited weapons include certain instruments used in selfdefence sports. Also prohibited are silencers, grenades and explosive-filled bottles and canisters, along with weapons that discharge gas, mace or any liquid or spray capable of incapacitating a person.
Restricted weapons include all manner of pistols and hand-guns-basically any weapon that can normally be aimed and fired by the action of one hand-and any firearm that is less than 26 inches in length or that can be adapted to be fired when reduced to a length of less than 26 inches by folding or telescoping. Restricted, also, are automatic weapons.
There are at present a number of methods of regulating restricted firearms. Firstly, with regard to criminal penal-

ties for illegal use, in common with all firearms there are sections of the code attaching a penalty to their improper use. For example, it is an offence to possess any firearm "for a purpose dangerous to the public peace or for the purpose of committing an offence", to use the words of section 83, or while attending or on the way to attend a public meeting-section 84-or to point at another person a firearm, whether loaded or unloaded, as per section 86. Secondly, with regard to prohibiting possession of firearms, another provision applicable to all firearms is section 95 of the code which allows the court to prohibit any person convicted of an offence involving a firearm from possessing a firearm for up to five years. Thirdly, all restricted weapons must be registered. This means that the RCMP commissioner keeps a central registry of all restricted weapons. That provision is made in sections 98 and 99. The commissioner operates through local registrars who, according to the code, have no authority to refuse registration unless there is no serial number on the gun.
The discretion to refuse registration is, in law, exercised only by the commissioner who may refuse to issue a registration certificate where he has notice of any matter that may render it desirable in the interests of the safety of other persons that the applicant should not possess a restricted weapon. This provision is to be found in section 99(4). In practice, however, some local registrars refuse to register an applicant's weapon. Moreover, the techniques of registration also vary across the country; for example, in one city a fee is required.
The mechanics of registration are, in the typical case, as follows. Firstly, a hand-gun is selected at a sporting goods store. Secondly, the would-be purchaser goes to the local registrar of firearms and applies for a registration certificate and a special permit to bring the gun to the local registrar. Thirdly, the purchaser then goes back to the store with the permit and returns to the local registrar with the gun. Fourthly, the local registrar then causes inquiries to be made into the character of the applicant. The gun is often kept by the registrar during this period. Fifthly, the registration application is then sent to the RCMP commissioner with any recommendations from the local registrar. Sixthly, if the commissioner issues a certificate after further checks by the RCMP-the RCMP checks on whether he has a criminal record, whether there is an order of prohibition against him and whether the gun has been stolen-the owner of the gun returns to the local registrar to pick up his gun, if the gun has been held there.
Registration certificates are granted to anyone who wishes to have a hand-gun in his home or business unless, as previously pointed out, the commissioner knows that it is "desirable in the interests of the safety of other persons that the applicant should not possess a restricted weapon". Subject to this condition, a person can keep a hand-gun at home if he wants it for protection, or because he is a collector or is simply starting a collection.
Permits to carry restricted weapons outside the home are much more carefully regulated. Here, the local registrar, assuming he is the person authorized to perform this function under section 97(1) of the code, has discretion to refuse to issue a permit. The section says "may be issued". No appeal can be taken from a refusal to grant such a permit, although an appeal to a magistrate can be taken if
March 30, 1976

a permit is revoked or if a registration certificate is not granted, as set out in section 99(6). The registrar will, of course, consider the character of the applicant. The registrar must also be satisfied, under section 97(2), that the applicant requires the restricted weapon for one of four stated purposes: to protect life or property; for use in connection with his lawful profession or occupation; for use in target practice under the auspices of a shooting club approved by the attorney general; or for use in target practise in accordance with the conditions attached to the permit. The practice varies from province to province. For example, some provinces make it very difficult to obtain a permit to carry a hand-gun "to protect life or property''; others are less restrictive.
A permit is needed to sell, repair or take in pawn a restricted weapon. Again, discretion is given to the registrar to refuse to issue a permit, as provided in sections 97(4) and 99(3), if he "has notice of any matter that may render it desirable in the interests of the safety of other persons that such a permit should not be issued to the applicant". In this case, if a permit is refused an appeal can be taken to a magistrate. Unrestricted weapons refer to all shotguns and rifles of a kind commonly used for hunting or sporting purposes. Neither registration certificate nor permits are required for these weapons, although a provincial licence is necessary in order to hunt game.
The aim of more gun control as advocated by the government and certain groups is to make Canada a better place to live in by reducing the violent crime rate. In this regard, the following extract from the Canadian Association of Chiefs of Police position paper on gun control is interesting to note:
Few authorities will dispute the statement that crime with violence is generally on the increase virtually throughout the world. Such crime with violence is identified with the use of explosives and weapons of all kinds, particularly firearms. For this reason, governments and individuals have shown increased interest in the control of firearms as one remedial measure probably because reported crime frequently associates the use of firearms.
What is identified today as being "the problem" is the number of violent crimes that are being committed and with which wrongly or rightly a firearm is being identified. There is no doubt that revolvers, pistols, "sawed-off" shotguns and "Saturday night specials" as well as any other kind of firearm imaginable have been involved in the commission of violent crime. The traditional sporting rifle whether suitable for high-powered shell or shot has also been involved. It must not be forgotten that violent crime is also committed with stilettos, butcher knives, chains, hammers and lead pipes, to name but a few other instruments.
The problem at hand is the high incidence of crime and the search for the methods of reducing it. If this can be achieved by the elimination of a weapon from the market then so much the better but this approach can be discarded from the very beginning because violent crime can be committed with any number of weapons.
Any restriction or control of firearms may in effect lessen the safeguards of society.
It is claimed that registration, control, prohibiting the sale of firearms or, as a most drastic step, stopping the manufacturing thereof would prove to be a safeguard to society. In the first instance a good proportion of legitimate users would be deprived of a rather enjoyable pastime: secondly, the firearms manufacturing industry would suffer considerably and the armed forces as well as security services would have to establish other means of procuring weapons in any case; thirdly, the highly desirable training facilities for the younger element, which facilities are yet grossly underdeveloped, would be eliminated thereby depriving society of a potential reserve of qualified marksmen.
Measures Against Crime
The strongest support of this point can be found in Switzerland where is no restrictive legislation whatever to curb the general use of firearms of any kind. In no country of Europe is the use of firearms more common and general. Every able bodied adult male is required by law to possess and know how to use military rifles. In addition, he may own as many pistols as he likes. In no country of the world is rifle and pistol shooting more universally indulged in by all classes of people. In spite of all these facts in no country in Europe, with the possible exception of England, are crimes of violence so rare as they are in Switzerland. This fact must give pause to the advocates of pistol prohibition as a crime preventive. Inanimate objects such as pistols, knives, axes or clubs do not and cannot cause crime. They do not and they cannot supply the motive or the impulse. The causes of crime must be sought elsewhere, in greed, hatred, jealousy and general moral depravity-and the remedy- if there any be, is more likely to be found in morals and education in improved police methods of detection, and in the more prompt and certain imposition of punishment. This is safeguarding society.
Although gun control proposals pretend to be directed toward the laudatory objective of reducing the incidence of violent crime, they tend in fact to aggravate the very conditions fostering crime by diverting attention away from the dismal failure of the criminal justice system to adequately cope with criminality. In point of fact, as a society we have simply failed to provide an efficient means whereby criminals can be apprehended, speedily prosecuted, reliably convicted, jailed and kept in jail.
The glaring failure of gun control laws significantly to affect the criminal element, as well as the reasons therefor, can be graphically portrayed by examining the experience of the city of Chicago. It has been estimated that there are presently some 20,000 gun laws in the United States, a number of which are operational in Chicago. The national federal firearms acts were on the federal books since their enactment in the 1930s, and the federal gun control act of 1968 eliminated interstate mail order sales of guns. Since 1968, Illinois has required a licence to purchase or possess either firearms or ammunition; additionally, Chicago residents have been required to register with the city authorities every firearm they own.
In 1965, before there was either a city registration ordinance of a state licensing law, 395 persons were murdered in Chicago. In 1973, five years after the enactment of those two new laws to "control guns", a record number of 864 persons were murdered in Chicago, and 1974 recorded nearly 1,000 murders. Anti-gun proposals are based on the faulty assumption that the increased sale of firearms in recent years constitutes, in and of itself, a basic cause of crime, when it would be far more rational to conclude that the sale of guns is to a significant degree merely an effect of the public's fear of rising crime.
The public has become increasingly alarmed and apprehensive over what it perceives as the open and notorious contempt shown by lawless elements, not only toward the law but toward the police and even the courts, all of which contributes toward the determination of law-abiding citizens to restore to themselves the means of doing that which they fear government either can no longer, or will no longer, do for them, namely, protect the safety and lives of their families as well as their property. Criminals will always manage to find guns. Stricter gun control laws may only provoke the existence of a black market for guns used for criminal ends.
The views of generally decent and law-abiding citizens are easy to describe. People have the right to bear arms for pleasure and self-protection, without interference from big

March 30, 1976
Measures Against Crime
government. Criminals will get guns, despite gun control laws. All gun control proposals-whether they advocate registration, licensing, record-keeping or anything else- are undesirable because they will inevitably lead to other, more restrictive measures.
As we have noted, Canada does have sufficient legislation already in existence to regulate legitimate firearms' use and traffic, and the police have interpreted and enforced the laws in a manner consistent with the attitude of the Canadian public. Because of the discretion of the police forces, relatively few Canadians are actually aware of the comprehensive manner in which firearms' usage has already been legislated. The present system regarding restricted weapons appears to be working reasonably well. Most police forces conduct a careful examination of the applicant before forwarding a recommendation to the RCMP for a registration certificate. The RCMP themselves make a routine check. Moreover, many local registrars tend to make it difficult for a person to obtain a permit to carry a hand-gun unless he is a bona fide target-shooter. The very fact that relatively few hand-guns are used in crimes in Canada, in comparison with their use in the United States, is some indication of the effectiveness of the system. The number of hand-guns in Canada is still relatively low.
Since we in Canada already have so many laws governing the use of offensive weapons, one must be reminded that no matter what possible strategy for control may be suggested, any further registration would require a considerable increase to an already overburdened administrative structure and would further tax the capabilities of police forces and the judicial system. Thus, it is emphasized in the Canadian Association of Chiefs of Police position paper on gun control laws that if there is to be any further legislation instituted for restricting the use of firearms even more than presently exists in Canada, its administration must be given first consideration, and if it be found that it cannot properly be administered, then it is far better to remain with the legislation that presently exists.
What effect would this compulsory licensing system have, for all persons who possess or propose to acquire firearms or ammunition, in keeping firearms out of the hands of criminals? The effect would be so insignificant that it would not begin to compensate for the expenditure of police time. Furthermore, good citizens, hunters, farmers, trappers and competitive marksmen would be forced to comply with an irritating, time-consuming and useless regulation.
It is contended by some that registration of rifles and shotguns, and the application of a permit system, would reduce certain types of manslaughter or murder such as those arising from domestic quarrels, property disputes and the onset of insanity. But it should be pointed out that people involved in such killings are usually those who have not been looked upon or recorded as criminals. They would have had no trouble in registering their firearms and securing permits to carry them.
In conclusion, the questions surrounding firearms and the correlation of violence are extremely complicated and often ambiguous. The available literature on the subject

indicates that research results often have been conveniently misinterpreted to suit the needs of those holding opposing points of view. The relationship between firearms and violence, however, does tend to obscure two other important facts bearing on the firearms question. First, it must be recognized that the vast majority of gun owners recognize the desirability of the proper use of firearms. It is indicated in the literature that most gun owners are law-abiding sportsmen and exemplary citizens who deplore the criminal use of firearms; and this being the case, their needs must sensitively be taken into account. Second, one must never lose sight of the fact that the root causes of violence may well go much deeper than mere widespread gun ownership. It must be recognized that firearms merely facilitate, rather than cause, some forms of violence.

This afternoon I would like to give some of my observations on the amendments in the bill which deal with gun control. It is interesting and revealing that the major portion of this bill is actually called "gun control." The government literature on this legislation calls it "gun control." I think that reveals a great deal of the government's real intentions on this subject. Maybe "gun control" sounds better than "people control", which is what this bill is really about. But it is odd that the advocates of gun control of one sort or another hardly ever talk about crime control or criminal control. This bill and this debate is really about gun control, even though the government has tried to pretend that it is about measures to protect society from crime. The gun control provisions make up 39 of the bill's 73 pages and actually constitute a new gun control law. Therefore, I am gcing to talk about gun control for a few minutes.
The fact is that Canada has some of the toughest gun control laws of any country in the world for certain categories of firearms. Nor are they new. Gun registration was introduced in Canada in 1935. The notorious hand-gun is a restricted weapon in this country and it is difficult to imagine how it could be any more controlled. A hand-gun must first be registered with the RCMP. This registration is not automatic, and can be refused. To remove the gun from the place of purchase, the owner must next obtain a "convenience permit" which only authorizes him to transport the gun to his home or the place of business for which the gun is registered. To transport the gun, again he must be issued with a "carrying permit" which will only be issued under strict provisions such as that the gun is necessary to protect life and property, that its use is in connection with the applicant's lawful profession or occupation, that it will be used on the premises of an approved shooting club, or that it will be used for target practise in accordance with the conditions attached to the permit.
March 30, 1976

These types of provisions governing certain restricted weapons, including hand-guns, were written into our Criminal Code over 40 years ago. At that time, so we are told, those who instituted this program had high hopes, although it is not exactly clear just what the hopes were for. Maybe they were negative hopes. Maybe they hoped that these controls would prevent the emergence of a Canadian John Dillinger or Ma Barker; I do not know.
May I call it five o'clock, Mr. Speaker?
